design_detail: CDC surveillance report (MMWR) with two analyses. (1) SUDORS, the State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System: unintentional and undetermined-intent overdose deaths in 49 states and the District of Columbia, January 2021 to June 2024, pooled (309,274 deaths; a jurisdiction had to report at least 75% of its overdose deaths in at least one 6-month period, and four were included for only part of the period), with a drug counted as involved when the medical examiner or coroner listed it as a cause of death on the death certificate, in their report or in the postmortem toxicology report; percentages of deaths involving any stimulant, methamphetamine and cocaine, with and without opioids, and decedents' characteristics and circumstances (46 states and DC with circumstance data). (2) NVSS, the National Vital Statistics System: all US death certificates, 2018–2023 (520,525 overdose deaths), age-adjusted rates of deaths with the multiple-cause codes for cocaine (T40.5) and for psychostimulants with abuse potential (T43.6), overall and by race and ethnicity, with and without opioid codes.
can_establish: What share of overdose deaths in nearly all US states in January 2021 to June 2024 involved methamphetamine as named by medical examiners, coroners and toxicology, how many of these also involved opioids, how decedents with and without opioid involvement differed in what was recorded about them, and how national age-adjusted death rates coded as involving psychostimulants changed from 2018 to 2023.
cannot_establish: Death rates among people who use methamphetamine (no denominator of use); that methamphetamine caused each death (involvement means listed as causing or contributing); any change over time in the methamphetamine-specific SUDORS figures (one pooled period, with jurisdictions entering for different periods); or whether opioid co-use was intentional (the report infers this from drug-checking studies, not from its own data).

sample.recruitment: Registries. SUDORS: CDC funds 49 states and DC under Overdose Data to Action to report unintentional and undetermined-intent overdose deaths from death certificates, postmortem toxicology and medical examiner or coroner reports; deaths are identified by underlying-cause codes X40–X44 and Y10–Y14 and by text searches of the cause-of-death fields (Methods › Data Sources, 1st paragraph; main-text footnote †). NVSS: death certificates for all US deaths (Methods › Data Sources, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: SUDORS: a jurisdiction had to report at least 75% of its overdose deaths in at least one 6-month period; all except California, Texas, Wisconsin and Wyoming reported for the whole period; California and Wisconsin are included for part of it, Texas and Wyoming only for January–June 2024, and North Dakota (not funded) not at all (main-text footnote †††). Circumstance analyses: 46 states and DC with circumstance data for at least 75% of deaths in at least one 6-month period (California, Idaho, North Dakota and Texas are not on the list); in those jurisdictions 93.1% of deaths had circumstance data (main-text footnotes §§§ and ¶¶¶). NVSS: underlying cause X40–X44 or Y10–Y14, with multiple-cause codes T40.5 for cocaine, T43.6 for psychostimulants with abuse potential (which the authors say primarily includes methamphetamine and other amphetamines) and T40.0–T40.4 and T40.6 for opioids (Methods › Data Sources, 2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Methamphetamine-involved SUDORS deaths: 72.2% male; aged 25–34 20.3%, 35–44 29.4%, 45–54 23.1%, 55–64 18.5%, 65 or older 5.1%; non-Hispanic White 74.2%, non-Hispanic Black 10.4%, Hispanic or Latino 10.2%, non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native 2.5% (Table). Aged 45 or older: 64% of those without opioids against 39% of those with opioids (19,350 of 30,124 and 25,770 of 66,463 with known age; editors' calculation from the Table).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (registry counts). Missing data: age and sex under 0.1%, race and ethnicity 1.0%; circumstance variables up to 3.0% (Table footnotes ** and ¶¶).
sample.selection_effects: SUDORS covers almost every state but four of them only for part of the period and North Dakota not at all, so the pooled percentages weight jurisdictions by the periods they reported; circumstance analyses leave out four states. The authors expect stimulant-involved deaths to be undercounted, because some are certified with cardiovascular causes and get no overdose code, and because toxicology testing varies and does not routinely cover emerging stimulants (Discussion › Limitations).

exposure.measurement: SUDORS: a drug counts as involved if the medical examiner or coroner listed it as a cause of death on the death certificate, in the medical examiner or coroner report or in the postmortem toxicology report (main-text footnote §§; Table footnote *); methamphetamine is named specifically. NVSS: the multiple-cause code T43.6, psychostimulants with abuse potential, which the authors describe as primarily methamphetamine and other amphetamines, so it is not specific to methamphetamine.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. A history of methamphetamine use was recorded for 32.9% of methamphetamine-involved decedents with circumstance data (43.8% of those without opioids, 28.1% with opioids) (Table).
exposure.polysubstance: Opioid co-involvement is the main stratifier: 68.8% of methamphetamine-involved deaths also involved opioids. 3.8% of all overdose deaths involved both methamphetamine and cocaine, and the methamphetamine and cocaine columns of the Table overlap (Table footnote *). Other co-involved drugs (alcohol, sedatives) are not reported; the only-stimulants category (14.5%) excludes deaths in which other drugs contributed (Figure 1 footnote **).

comparison.controls: None: descriptive comparisons between deaths with and without opioid involvement, between stimulant types, between racial and ethnic groups and across years.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (registry counts). Recorded circumstances such as a history of cardiovascular disease, treatment or homelessness depend on investigative reports and are probably underestimated (Discussion › Limitations, third limitation).

outcomes.instruments: Death certificates, medical examiner and coroner reports and postmortem toxicology (SUDORS); death certificates coded with ICD-10 (NVSS); age-adjusted rates per 100,000 standardized to the 2000 US standard population (main-text footnote ¶¶).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors name five limitations: deaths certified with cardiovascular causes in the setting of stimulant toxicity may get no overdose code and be missed; postmortem toxicology testing varies and does not routinely cover emerging stimulants (both causing underestimation); circumstance information depends on investigative reports; race and ethnicity may be misclassified; and some large states are excluded from the circumstance analyses (Discussion › Limitations).
outcomes.operationalization: Stimulant-involved death: cocaine, methamphetamine, other amphetamines, synthetic cathinones, prescription stimulants or any other central nervous system stimulant listed as causing or contributing (SUDORS; Methods › Data Sources, 1st paragraph); in NVSS, cocaine (T40.5) or psychostimulants with abuse potential (T43.6). Opioid co-involvement: an opioid also listed (SUDORS) or coded (NVSS). Prescription stimulants include amphetamine and dextroamphetamine only when methamphetamine is not detected (main-text footnote **).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive percentages and rates are reported without statistical tests or confidence intervals.

analysis.effect_sizes: SUDORS, January 2021–June 2024, 309,274 overdose deaths: any stimulant 182,502 (59.0%), with opioids 133,293 (43.1%), without opioids 49,209 (15.9%); methamphetamine 96,614 (31.2%), with opioids 66,475 (21.5% of all deaths; 68.8% of methamphetamine-involved deaths), without opioids 30,139 (9.7% of all deaths; 31.2% of methamphetamine-involved deaths, editors' calculation); cocaine 92,697 (30.0%), 79.1% of them with opioids; methamphetamine and cocaine together 3.8%; prescription stimulants 1.6%, synthetic cathinones 0.7%, MDMA or MDA 0.4%; only stimulants 14.5% (Results › SUDORS, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table, Overall row; Figure 1). Methamphetamine-involved deaths with circumstance data (67,831), without against with opioids: known history of cardiovascular disease 39.3% vs 19.8%; seen in an emergency department for the fatal overdose 30.3% vs 17.4%; evidence of opioid use history 12.2% vs 41.1%; ever treated for mental health or substance use disorders 14.2% vs 24.0%; homelessness or housing instability 15.7% vs 18.9%; naloxone given 15.6% vs 27.1% (Table). NVSS age-adjusted rates per 100,000, 2018 and 2023: psychostimulants 3.9 and 10.4, cocaine 4.5 and 8.6; psychostimulants among non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native people 11.0 and 32.9 and among non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander people 7.4 and 16.3; cocaine among non-Hispanic Black people 9.1 and 24.3 (Results › NVSS, 1st paragraph). Counts cited from an NCHS data brief: psychostimulant-involved deaths 2,266 in 2011 and 34,855 in 2023, cocaine-involved 4,681 and 29,449 (Introduction). No confidence intervals anywhere.
analysis.covariates: None. NVSS rates are age-adjusted; SUDORS percentages are crude.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Surveillance report; reviewed by CDC and deemed not research (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: The NVSS trends with and without opioids, overall and for White, Asian and Hispanic people, are shown only in Figure 2 and a Supplementary Figure (an image and a separate file, not read); the text says only that the largest increases in every group were in deaths also involving opioids, without figures. The SUDORS figures are pooled over 3.5 years, so no trend in the methamphetamine-specific share is given. Provisional declines in 2024 are mentioned without figures (Introduction; Discussion, 4th paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Methamphetamine was involved in 31.2% of overdose deaths in 49 states and DC in January 2021 to June 2024; about two-thirds of these deaths (68.8%) also involved opioids, and 30,139 (9.7% of all overdose deaths) did not. Decedents without opioids were older and more often had a recorded history of cardiovascular disease. National age-adjusted death rates coded as involving psychostimulants rose from 3.9 to 10.4 per 100,000 between 2018 and 2023, with the largest increases among American Indian or Alaska Native people and, by the text's account, in deaths also involving opioids.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary and most of the discussion describe the data accurately. Three statements go beyond them: (1) that drug-checking programmes rarely found opioids in stimulant products, suggesting that people who died with both had intentionally used separate products (Discussion, 4th paragraph), an inference from other studies, not from these deaths; (2) that stable survey prevalence among American Indian or Alaska Native and Black people "suggests increased drug potency or differential access" to care (Discussion, 6th paragraph), from survey tables the report does not analyse; (3) that the 38.7% with a known history of cardiovascular disease among deaths with stimulants and no opioids, against about 10% of all US adults, possibly reflects long-term stimulant use (Discussion, 2nd and 5th paragraphs): the comparison is not age-standardized, although two-thirds of these decedents were 45 or older, and history of hypertension is excluded from the decedents' figure (Table footnote ***). The recommendations (contingency management, low-barrier care, naloxone and stimulant overdose education) rest on cited guidance, not on the report's data.

timeline.event: Analysis of the same national death records for ages 18–64, 2015–2019: deaths with the code for psychostimulants other than cocaine rose from 5,526 to 15,489, more than half of the 2019 deaths with opioids

Spencer, Miniño and Garnett (2023), NCHS Data Brief 474, opioid co-involvement in deaths involving cocaine and psychostimulants, 2011–2021, cited here for the rise in stimulant deaths without opioids; not read
Garnett and Miniño (2024), NCHS Data Brief 522, drug overdose deaths 2003–2023, the source of this report's 2011 and 2023 counts; not read

Analysis of the same national death records, all ages, 1999–2023: 34,855 methamphetamine-involved deaths in 2023, the same number this report gives for deaths coded as involving psychostimulants (T43.6), which suggests that the later analysis used that code (editors' inference)
This report: methamphetamine named in 31.2% of SUDORS overdose deaths, January 2021–June 2024, 68.8% of them with opioids

replication.where_it_stands: The NVSS part re-analyses the same national death records as Han et al. (2021) and Zhu et al. (2025), so its trend is not independent replication. The SUDORS part draws on a partly separate source (medical examiner, coroner and toxicology reports, naming methamphetamine specifically) and is the first source read for this page that gives the share of methamphetamine-involved overdose deaths with and without opioids, for one pooled period.

funding.funder: No funding statement; a CDC report written by staff of the Division of Overdose Prevention, National Center for Injury Prevention and Control. SUDORS is funded by CDC through the Overdose Data to Action in States programme (Methods › Data Sources, 1st paragraph; author affiliations).
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors completed the ICMJE form for disclosure of potential conflicts of interest; no potential conflicts of interest were disclosed.
funding.affiliations_note: All eight authors are CDC staff (Division of Overdose Prevention). The agency that runs the surveillance system and funds the state overdose-prevention programmes wrote the report and its recommendations; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Methamphetamine-specific, toxicology-based death surveillance with complete and stable jurisdiction coverage, reported year by year rather than pooled, with intervals, the counts with and without opioids for each year, and a denominator of people who use methamphetamine from surveys of the same years.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: NVSS: all US death certificates. SUDORS: 49 states and DC, but four states only for part of the period and North Dakota not at all.
Complete counts of reported deaths, not samples.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Definitions, codes, inclusion rules by jurisdiction and missing data are given in footnotes.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Circumstance analyses leave out four states; jurisdictions enter for different 6-month periods, so the pooled percentages mix periods.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Medical examiner and coroner attribution with toxicology is the best routine source, but testing varies between jurisdictions and does not routinely cover emerging stimulants, and NVSS uses T43.6, which is not specific to methamphetamine.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Toxicology testing and certification practices vary within and across jurisdictions (Discussion › Limitations).
Descriptive percentages and age-adjusted rates suit the question, but no intervals or trend tests are given, and the opioid-stratified trends appear only in figures.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A large surveillance analysis whose definitions are stated in full. Its limits concern coverage (four states partly or not covered in SUDORS, four absent from the circumstance analyses), variable toxicology and certification, which the authors expect to undercount stimulant deaths, the non-specific T43.6 code in the trend analysis, and the absence of intervals. In the editors' reading, the undercount may fall more on deaths without opioids, since deaths certified as cardiovascular are the ones missed and decedents without opioids were older and more often had cardiovascular disease, so the share with opioids may be somewhat overstated. It may be cited for the share of methamphetamine-involved overdose deaths with and without opioids in January 2021 to June 2024, for decedents' recorded characteristics, and for the age-adjusted rates of deaths coded T43.6 in 2018 and 2023; not for rates among people who use methamphetamine, not for causes of death, and not as independent confirmation of the national death-record trend.

key_findings.finding: Data: SUDORS (49 states and DC; unintentional and undetermined-intent overdose deaths, January 2021–June 2024; a drug counted as involved when the medical examiner or coroner listed it as a cause of death on the death certificate, in their report or in the postmortem toxicology report) and NVSS (all US death certificates, 2018–2023; underlying cause X40–X44 or Y10–Y14 with multiple-cause codes T40.5 for cocaine, T43.6 for psychostimulants with abuse potential and T40.0–T40.4 and T40.6 for opioids; age-adjusted to the 2000 US standard population).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data Sources, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; main-text footnotes †, §§ and ¶¶ (the Table gives the involvement rule as its footnote *)

key_findings.finding: SUDORS coverage: a jurisdiction had to report at least 75% of its overdose deaths in at least one 6-month period; all but four reported for the whole period, California and Wisconsin were included for part of it, Texas and Wyoming only for January–June 2024, and North Dakota not at all. Circumstance analyses: 46 states and DC (226,698 deaths), with circumstance data for 93.1% of deaths in those jurisdictions.
key_findings.locator: Main-text footnotes †††, §§§ and ¶¶¶ (the Table gives the same rules as its footnotes § and §§); Table, circumstance-data row

key_findings.finding: Of 309,274 overdose deaths, 59.0% involved any stimulant, 31.2% methamphetamine and 30.0% cocaine; 3.8% both methamphetamine and cocaine; prescription stimulants 1.6%, synthetic cathinones 0.7%, MDMA or MDA 0.4%. 73.0% of stimulant-involved deaths co-involved opioids, including 79.1% of cocaine-involved and 68.8% of methamphetamine-involved deaths; 14.5% of deaths involved only stimulants.
key_findings.locator: Results › SUDORS: Stimulant-Involved Overdose Deaths During January 2021–June 2024, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 (image; values not extracted beyond the text)

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine-involved deaths: 96,614 (31.2% of all overdose deaths), of which 66,475 (21.5% of all deaths) co-involved opioids and 30,139 (9.7% of all deaths) did not. Any stimulant: 182,502 (59.0%), with opioids 133,293 (43.1%), without opioids 49,209 (15.9%).
key_findings.locator: Table, Overall (49 states and DC) row; Results › SUDORS, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Without opioids = 31.2% of methamphetamine-involved deaths (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Age of methamphetamine-involved decedents: 45–54 23.1%, 55–64 18.5%, 65 or older 5.1% overall; among those without opioids 27.1%, 27.9% and 9.2%; among those with opioids 21.3%, 14.3% and 3.2%. For any stimulant, 66.5% of decedents without opioids and 44.2% of those with opioids were 45 or older. About 72% of methamphetamine-involved decedents were male.
key_findings.locator: Table, Age group and Sex rows (methamphetamine columns); Results › SUDORS, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Aged 45 or older: 64% without opioids vs 39% with opioids among methamphetamine-involved deaths with known age (editors' calculation from the Table).

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine-involved deaths with circumstance data (67,831), without vs with opioids: known history of cardiovascular disease (hypertension excluded) 39.3% vs 19.8%; seen in an emergency department for the fatal overdose 30.3% vs 17.4%; evidence of opioid use history 12.2% vs 41.1%; ever treated for mental health or substance use disorders 14.2% vs 24.0%; homelessness or housing instability 15.7% vs 18.9%. The text reports these contrasts for any stimulant (38.7% vs 21.2% cardiovascular disease) and says the methamphetamine and cocaine patterns were comparable.
key_findings.locator: Table, circumstance rows (methamphetamine columns) and footnote ***; Results › SUDORS, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: These contrasts are crude: decedents without opioids were also older (64% vs 39% aged 45 or older among all methamphetamine-involved deaths; editors' calculation), so part of the difference in cardiovascular history may reflect age (editors' note).

key_findings.finding: NVSS age-adjusted overdose death rates per 100,000: psychostimulants with abuse potential 3.9 in 2018 and 10.4 in 2023; cocaine 4.5 and 8.6. Psychostimulants among non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native people 11.0 and 32.9, among non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander people 7.4 and 16.3; cocaine among non-Hispanic Black people 9.1 and 24.3. Across groups, the largest increases were in deaths co-involving stimulants and opioids (no figures in the text).
key_findings.locator: Results › NVSS: Trends in Stimulant-Involved Overdose Death Rates from 2018 to 2023, 1st paragraph; Abstract; Figure 2 and Supplementary Figure (not read)

key_findings.finding: Counts cited from an NCHS data brief: overdose deaths involving psychostimulants with abuse potential 2,266 in 2011 and 34,855 in 2023; cocaine 4,681 and 29,449. Provisional data show declines in 2024 (no figures).

Limitations named by the authors: stimulant overdose deaths certified with cardiovascular causes may lack overdose codes and be missed; postmortem toxicology varies and emerging stimulants are not tested routinely (both lead to underestimation); circumstance information depends on investigative reports; race and ethnicity may be misclassified; some large states are excluded from the circumstance analyses.

The discussion infers intentional co-use of separate stimulant and opioid products from drug-checking studies that rarely found opioids in stimulant samples, and compares the 38.7% cardiovascular history of decedents with stimulants and no opioids with about 10% of all US adults, possibly representing long-term stimulant use.
